title: Banned AI verbs
summary: A stable set of verbs (delve, leverage, utilize, facilitate, ...) is statistically overrepresented in AI text across every reference corpus; plain equivalents exist for each.

source.rule: "Empower" / "leverage" / "unlock" — say what you actually mean; "Seamless" / "seamlessly" — nothing is seamless

tests.label: banned verb fails
tests.input: We leverage the framework to streamline deployment.

tests.label: plain verb passes
tests.input: We use the framework to speed up deployment.

notes: Literal technical uses are context-sensitive; e.g. 'navigate the website' is acceptable, 'navigate the regulatory process' is not (see ZS-PROSE-067 exclusion zones).

title: Banned AI adjectives
summary: Robust, comprehensive, pivotal, seamless and friends are the most overused adjectives in AI text; they add fake gravitas where a plain word or a fact belongs.

tests.label: puff adjective fails
tests.input: The platform offers a seamless, transformative experience.

tests.label: plain adjective passes
tests.input: The platform loads pages in 200ms.

notes: Context-aware severity: 'a comprehensive audit by the FTC in 2024' is lower severity than 'a comprehensive examination of the issues' (named entity next to the word).

title: Metaphorical nouns (tapestry, realm, beacon, ...)
summary: AI injects false gravitas by using concrete nouns metaphorically ('a tapestry of regulations', 'a beacon of hope'); literal uses of the same words are fine.

source.rule: Overused metaphorical nouns / Metaphorical vs. literal distinction

tests.label: metaphorical use fails
tests.input: The startup is a beacon of hope in the AI landscape.

tests.label: literal use passes
tests.input: The lighthouse guides ships into the harbor.

notes: Requires bigram context: flag only metaphorical uses ('a tapestry of regulations'), not literal ones ('medieval tapestry', 'last will and testament', 'Arizona landscape').

title: Empty intensifiers and filler adverbs
summary: Extremely, dramatically, truly, literally and similar intensifiers are banned or flagged across all references; they inflate without proving. Keep only when they carry genuine emphasis or uncertainty.

tests.label: empty intensifier fails
tests.input: The results are extremely significant for the industry.

tests.label: no intensifier passes
tests.input: The build failed, and I watched the deploy roll back.

notes: Purpose-gate: 'I think', 'maybe', 'to be honest' stay when they express real uncertainty or the writer's spoken rhythm.

title: Academic AI tells
summary: Academic-sounding filler ('shed light on', 'a plethora of', 'prior to', 'in terms of') reads as AI even in non-academic prose; plain equivalents are shorter and clearer.

tests.label: academic tell fails
tests.input: The study sheds light on a myriad of prior findings.

tests.label: plain wording passes
tests.input: The study explains several earlier findings.

title: Banned opening phrases
summary: 'In today's fast-paced world', 'It's important to note that', 'Let's dive into' and kin are throat-clearing openers that delay the point; every reference bans them.

terms: it is important to note that

source.rule: "In this blog post, we will explore..." — be direct, just start

tests.label: throat-clearing opener fails
tests.input: In today's fast-paced world, teams need to move quickly.

tests.label: direct opener passes
tests.input: Teams ship faster when the build takes two minutes.

title: Banned transition phrases
summary: Furthermore, Moreover, That being said, At its core and similar connective filler are AI defaults; plain connectors (also, and, but, however, still) work better.

source.rule: Overused transitions / Transitional phrases to avoid
Filler transitions: "That being said," "It's worth noting that," "At the end of the day," "Without further ado," "As you might know"

tests.label: transition filler fails
tests.input: Furthermore, the fix is cheap; moreover, it is fast.

tests.label: plain connector passes
tests.input: The fix is cheap, and it is fast.

notes: Threshold context: if more than 30% of paragraphs in an article begin with a transition word or adverbial clause, the text is structurally artificial (see ZS-PROSE-053).

title: Banned concluding and summary phrases
summary: 'In conclusion', 'At the end of the day', 'Ultimately', 'Overall' announce a recap the reader just lived through; end on the last concrete point instead.

terms: at the end of the day

tests.label: summary opener fails
tests.input: In conclusion, the migration delivered real savings.

tests.label: direct close passes
tests.input: The migration cut monthly spend by $4,000.

title: Throat-clearing openers
summary: 'Here's the thing', 'Let me be clear', 'I'll be honest' promise substance the sentence then delivers anyway; cut them and state the point.

tests.label: throat-clearer fails
tests.input: Here's the thing: the gate is broken.

tests.label: point stated directly passes
tests.input: The gate is broken.

title: Faux-insight setups
summary: 'What most people get wrong', 'The part everyone misses', 'Here's what nobody tells you' flatter the writer as the lone expert; the claim should stand on its own.

terms: this is the part most people skip
here is what nobody tells you
what most people do not know

tests.label: faux-insight fails
tests.input: The part everyone misses: distribution is the real moat.

tests.label: claim stands alone passes
tests.input: Distribution is the moat.

title: Rhetorical setups
summary: 'What if I told you...', 'Think about it:', 'Plot twist:' and self-answered 'Question? Answer.' pairs manufacture drama; drop them and make the point.

source.rule: Rhetorical colon abuse ('Here's the thing:', 'Think about it:')

tests.label: rhetorical setup fails
tests.input: What if I told you the fix is already merged?

tests.label: plain statement passes
tests.input: The fix is already merged.

title: Weasel attribution
summary: 'Experts agree', 'industry reports suggest', 'studies show' hide an unverifiable claim behind a nameless authority; name the source or cut the claim.

source.rule: **Watch for:** experts argue, observers have cited, industry reports, some critics, several publications

tests.label: vague attribution fails
tests.input: Experts agree that remote work is here to stay.

tests.label: named source passes
tests.input: The 2025 Gallup survey found 61% of workers prefer remote days.

notes: If the writer has no source, flag for them to find one instead of inventing an attribution (fabricated attributions are an integrity-domain rule).

title: Corporate and marketing cliches
summary: 'Unlock the power of', 'Elevate your', 'Bridge the gap', 'Move the needle' are promotional filler that reads as templated; no-slop bans hype tone outright.

terms: take it to the next level

tests.label: marketing cliche fails
tests.input: Unlock the power of your data with our platform.

tests.label: plain claim passes
tests.input: Our platform queries a 40TB warehouse in under a second.

title: Formulaic email openers and closers
summary: 'I hope this email finds you well', 'As per my last email', 'Please don't hesitate to reach out' are boilerplate; write the substance instead.

terms: i hope this email finds you well
i hope this finds you well
please don't hesitate to reach out
please do not hesitate to reach out
do not hesitate to contact me

tests.label: email boilerplate fails
tests.input: I hope this email finds you well. Please don't hesitate to reach out.

tests.label: direct email passes
tests.input: The invoice is attached; payment is due Friday.

title: Collaborative narrator language
summary: 'Let's explore', 'we will examine', 'as we can see' stage a guided tour instead of stating the fact; no-slop bans collaborative language outright.

source.rule: 5) AI tells and meta commentary — No: "In this essay" / "This piece explores" / "As a writer" / "We will discuss" / "Here are the key takeaways"

tests.label: tour-guide opener fails
tests.input: Let's explore how the queue drains under load.

tests.label: direct statement passes
tests.input: The queue drains at 2,000 messages per second under load.

title: 'Whether you're' and 'By [gerund]' openers
summary: 'Whether you're a X, Y, or Z' and 'By understanding X, you can Y' are structural AI formulas that open with audience flattery or an empty promise.

source.rule: Banned phrases ('Whether you're a [X] or a [Y]...', 'From X to Y')

tests.label: whether-formula fails
tests.input: Whether you're a startup or a giant, this guide is for you.

tests.label: gerund formula fails
tests.input: By understanding the queue, you can cut latency.

tests.label: direct sentence passes
tests.input: The queue drains faster when you batch writes.

title: Inflated symbolism phrases
summary: Multi-word phrases like 'provide a valuable insight', 'left an indelible mark', 'serves as a testament' appear hundreds of times more often in AI text than human baselines (isgpt.org corpus analysis, 2025).

terms: play a significant role in shaping

tests.label: inflated symbolism fails
tests.input: Her mentorship left an indelible mark on the team.

tests.label: concrete claim passes
tests.input: Her mentorship cut the team's onboarding time in half.

title: Banned response openers
summary: 'Certainly,', 'Great question!', 'As an AI...', 'Moreover,' at the start of a reply are model-first-word tells shared across ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, Gemini and DeepSeek fingerprints.

source.rule: Banned sentence/paragraph openers and model-specific first-word tells
Great question! Here is an overview of the French Revolution. ... I hope this helps! Let me know if you'd like me to expand on any section.

tests.label: response opener fails
tests.input: Certainly, let me explain how caching works.

tests.label: direct answer passes
tests.input: Caching stores query results so repeat calls skip the database.

title: Em dash cap: max 1 per 500 words
summary: The em dash is the single most cited AI tell in existence; cap at one per 500 words, and prefer commas, colons, parentheses, or new sentences.

source.rule: Em dashes: Maximum ONE per 500 words
Em dashes (1-2 in longer drafts only)
Rule 1: No emdashes / Em Dashes: The Primary AI Tell
Em dash discipline (max one per paragraph)

The final rewrite must not contain em dashes (—) or en dashes (–) unless the writer's sample uses them; then match the sample's rate. ... This includes spaced dashes and double hyphens (` -- `) used as dashes.
LAW 3 - NO EM-DASHES OR EN-DASHES. Use ` - ` throughout the body, key patterns, and invitation. Preserve a source's literal dash inside a direct quote.
Em-dash overuse (density; 2+ in a sentence; spaced pairs as drama) | Commas, periods, parentheses; ≤1 per ~150 words; zero on LinkedIn

tests.label: over cap fails
tests.input: It's not X — it's Y — and never Z — period.

tests.label: single dash passes
tests.input: One dash — only.

notes: In short copy use none; in longer drafts 1-2 are fine when they clearly beat commas or parentheses. Remove clusters and decorative dashes.

title: Exclamation mark cap: max 1 per 1,000 words
summary: Exclamation marks manufacture enthusiasm; cap at one per 1,000 words because enthusiasm should come from word choice.

source.rule: Exclamation marks: maximum one per 1,000 words

tests.label: over cap fails
tests.input: Wow! Amazing! Incredible! Fantastic!

tests.label: none passes
tests.input: The gate closed at 5pm and held.

notes: Exclude exclamation marks inside code, URLs, and quoted material.

title: Ellipsis cap: max 1 per piece
summary: Ellipses only when genuinely trailing off, never as a transition; at most one per piece.

source.rule: Ellipses: Only when genuinely trailing off. Never as transition. Max one per piece
check_type=types.ExistenceSimple(pattern=r"\.\.\.") message="'...' is an approximation, use the ellipsis symbol '…'."

tests.label: multiple ellipses fail
tests.input: I mean... it's fine... whatever...

tests.label: none passes
tests.input: She paused, then answered the question.

title: Colon reveals (dramatic colon)
summary: A noun phrase, a colon, then a lowercase dramatic reveal ('The best part: it learns.') fakes drama; use colons for lists, labels, and quotes, not mic-drop reveals.

source.rule: Colon reveals; sentence case after colon

tests.label: dramatic reveal fails
tests.input: The detail that makes it work: a separate agent grades it.

tests.label: list colon passes
tests.input: The report covers three areas: security, performance, and cost.

notes: Regex hint ':\s[a-z]' false-positives on legitimate list colons; triage decides. Prefer sentence case after a colon unless grammar, a proper noun, a title, or code requires otherwise.

title: Scare quotes on normal words
summary: Quotation marks around ordinary words imply they are fake or contested; use quotes only for actual quotations from a named source.

source.rule: Rule 10: No scare quotes on normal words

tests.label: scare quotes fail
tests.input: The 'revolutionary' feature shipped late.

tests.label: no quotes passes
tests.input: The feature shipped late.

notes: Do not flag text inside genuine quotations from cited sources (see ZS-PROSE-067).

title: Binary contrasts and contrasting parallelism
summary: 'It's not X. It's Y.' and 'The question isn't X, the issue is Y' simulate punchy emphasis; more than two contrasting parallelisms per 500 words is a high-confidence AI indicator.

matcher.pattern: \b(It's not (just )?[^.!?]{2,60}[.,] It's|The (question|issue) isn't [^.!?]{2,60}[.,] The (question|issue) is|not just [^.!?]{2,60}\. It's)\b

source.rule: Contrasting parallelism overuse (threshold: more than two per 500-word block)
2) "It's not X, it's Y" constructions — Ban the pattern and its masked variants, including: "This isn't about X. It's about Y." / "Not X but Y."
RE_NOT_BUT — "not X, but Y" contrast detector: \b(?:is not|are not|wasn't|aren't|not)\s+…[,;:]\s*but\s+ … ; 25% of the composite Slop Score is not-x-but-y contrast patterns
composite of slop words (60%), "not X, but Y" contrast patterns (25%), and slop trigrams (15%), min-max normalized against the model leaderboard, scaled 0–100. `> 25 = SLOP`

tests.label: binary contrast fails
tests.input: It's not a tool problem, it's a process problem.

tests.label: contrasting parallelism fails
tests.input: The question isn't the model, the question is the eval.

tests.label: direct claim passes
tests.input: The eval matters more than the model.

title: Negative listing
summary: 'Not a X. Not a Y. A Z.' is a rhetorical ladder that delays the point; just say Z.

tests.label: negative ladder fails
tests.input: Not a toy. Not a game. A tool.

tests.label: plain claim passes
tests.input: The device is a tool.

title: Rule of Three overuse
summary: AI defaults to triads; three-adjective or three-phrase lists as a rhetorical device signal AI even when vocabulary is clean.

source.rule: Ideas arrive in threes to sound complete, whether the meaning has three parts or not.
6) Symmetry padding — No three-part lists unless earned. No "X, Y, and Z" as decoration.
No Rule of Three. AI defaults to threes. Break it. Use two, four, one, five. Never default to three unless the content genuinely has three items.

tests.label: padded triad fails
tests.input: Fast, reliable, and affordable are what users want.

tests.label: genuine two-item list passes
tests.input: Fast and reliable are what users want.

notes: Purpose-gate: three items are fine when the content genuinely has three items.

title: 'Not just X, but Y' constructions
summary: 'It's not just X, but Y' / 'not only X, but also Y' are banned structural formulas that stage a false escalation.

source.rule: Banned phrases ('Not just X, but Y', 'It's not just about X — it's about Y')

tests.label: not-just-but fails
tests.input: It's not just a tool but a platform.

tests.label: not-only-but fails
tests.input: It's not only fast but also reliable.

tests.label: plain coordination passes
tests.input: It is a tool and a platform.

title: Superficial -ing clauses
summary: Trailing '-ing' clauses (highlighting, underscoring, reflecting, showcasing) pretend to explain meaning but add no information; replace with concrete consequences.

source.rule: **Watch for:** highlighting, underscoring, emphasizing, ensuring, reflecting, symbolizing, contributing to, cultivating, fostering, encompassing, showcasing

tests.label: -ing gloss fails
tests.input: The launch adds file search, highlighting the team's commitment.

tests.label: concrete result passes
tests.input: The launch adds file search, so users find old drafts.

title: Importance puffery
summary: 'Stands as a testament', 'marks a pivotal moment', 'plays a vital role' announce importance instead of demonstrating it; state the fact and let the reader judge.

tests.label: puffery fails
tests.input: The launch marks a pivotal moment for the company.

tests.label: fact stands alone passes
tests.input: The launch is the company's first paid product.

title: Interpretive metadiscourse
summary: Lines that step outside the subject to tell readers what to notice ('The key point is', 'As you can see', 'This distinction matters') are reader guidance the prose should do on its own.

terms: that last part matters more than it sounds

source.rule: Interpretive metadiscourse. Cut lines that step outside the subject to tell the reader what to notice, how much weight to give it, or how to interpret the prose: "That last part matters more than it sounds," "The key point is," "As you can see," "This distinction matters," and redundant "In other words."

tests.label: reader guidance fails
tests.input: As you can see, the build failed.

tests.label: support instead passes
tests.input: The build failed because the token expired.

notes: Purpose-gate: if the point is clear, delete the aside; otherwise replace it with support or facts already in the content.

title: Fake-strong copulas
summary: 'Serves as', 'stands as', 'boasts', 'ventured into' substitute for plain 'is'/'has' and inflate the sentence; prefer the copula.

tests.label: fake copula fails
tests.input: The library serves as a foundational component.

tests.label: plain copula passes
tests.input: The library is the base of the stack.

title: Synonym cycling (elegant variation)
summary: Rotating synonyms for the same referent ('the agent... the assistant... the tool') is a stylistic tic; repeat the clear word instead.

tests.label: rotating terms fails
tests.input: The agent reviews the draft. The assistant scores it. The tool suggests fixes.

tests.label: consistent term passes
tests.input: The agent reviews the draft, scores it, and suggests fixes.

title: Dramatic fragmentation
summary: 'X. And Y. And Z.' or 'That's it. That's the whole thing.' uses fragments for manufactured punch; use complete sentences.

matcher.pattern: \. And [A-Z][a-z]+\.|\. That's it\. That's the whole thing\.

tests.label: stacked fragments fail
tests.input: The gate jammed. And stuck. And broke.

tests.label: complete sentence passes
tests.input: The gate jammed, stuck, and broke.

notes: Human fragments used sparingly are fine; the stacked 'And'-chain pattern is the tell.

title: Robotic rhythm
summary: Repeated sentence shapes, identical paragraph structures, and stacked punchy fragments read mechanical; vary the shape when it helps the point.

tests.label: uniform shapes fail
tests.input: The gate opened. The gate closed. The gate jammed.

tests.label: varied rhythm passes
tests.input: The gate opened at 9, then jammed at noon when the latch bent.

title: Fake-profound kickers
summary: A final 'deep' line that turns the point into a metaphor or mic-drop aphorism is a tell; delete it and end on the clearest concrete sentence.

tests.label: mic-drop ending fails
tests.input: We fixed the bug. In the end, every bug is a lesson in humility.

tests.label: concrete ending passes
tests.input: We fixed the bug by adding a null check.

notes: Do not rewrite the kicker into a better metaphor; delete it and end on the last concrete point, takeaway, or next action.

title: Performative urgency
summary: 'Act now', 'don't miss out' without a concrete consequence is synthetic urgency; it needs a real deadline or penalty in the same sentence.

matcher.pattern: \b(act now|don't miss out|do not miss out|limited time only|act fast|hurry)\b

source.rule: Rule 9: No performative urgency without a reason

tests.label: baseless urgency fails
tests.input: Act now before it's too late.

tests.label: grounded deadline passes
tests.input: Orders placed by Friday ship Monday.

title: Research-process narration
summary: 'Could not be located', 'was not found', 'as of my last update' narrate the search instead of reporting facts; report what you can support and silently omit the rest.

source.rule: While specific details about the company's founding are not extensively documented in readily available sources, it appears to have been established sometime in the 1990s. ... Information about her early life is not publicly available, suggesting she maintains a low profile.
The figures below are drawn from each vendor's published pricing; anything we could not confirm is flagged rather than guessed.
source.ref: SKILL.md §25 (Writing about the document instead of its subject)

tests.label: search narration fails
tests.input: The document could not be located in the archive.

tests.label: fact only passes
tests.input: The document is archived under 2024-Q3.

notes: Also covers 'as of [date]' qualifiers attached to an inability to find something, and sections enumerating documents the writer could not obtain.

title: Reference narration
summary: 'As discussed above', 'as we will see' narrate the text's own structure; make the connection and move on.

source.rule: Rule 8: Reference without narrating the reference
items=("The preceeding discussion", "The rest of this article", "This chapter discusses", "The preceding paragraph demonstrated", "The previous section analyzed")

tests.label: self-reference fails
tests.input: As discussed above, the fix is shipped.

tests.label: direct statement passes
tests.input: The fix is shipped in v2.1.

title: Parataxis (stacked short declaratives)
summary: Three or more short declarative sentences in a row read like a poem and signal AI; connect related thoughts with clauses, conjunctions, or semicolons.

source.rule: No parataxis (three or more short declarative sentences in a row)
No parataxis. Parataxis is the AI default: short sentence. Then another. Then another. It reads like a poem and immediately signals AI authorship.

tests.label: staccato run fails
tests.input: Short sentence. Then another. Then another.

tests.label: connected thought passes
tests.input: AI chains short sentences together because it is easier than constructing a thought.

title: 'As [role], I...' openers
summary: 'As a developer, I...' announces credentials instead of making the point; real people just say the thing.

tests.label: credential opener fails
tests.input: As a developer, I recommend profiling first.

tests.label: direct claim passes
tests.input: Profile first, then optimize.

title: Hedging seesaw
summary: Giving a counterpoint equal weight and then not committing is the AI default; pick a side and acknowledge counterpoints in one sentence max.

tests.label: seesaw fails
tests.input: Option A is best. But option B has merit. Still, A might win.

tests.label: committed claim passes
tests.input: Option A is best for three reasons.

title: Passive voice
summary: Passive constructions ('was killed', 'is being done') read dead; write-good flags them as 'may be passive voice'.

source.rule: The text hides who acts or drops the subject. Use active voice when it makes the actor and action clearer.
message: "'%s' may be passive voice. Use active voice if you can." raw: - \b(am|are|were|being|is|been|was|be)\b\s* tokens: - '[\w]+ed'

tests.label: passive fails
tests.input: The script was killed.

tests.label: active passes
tests.input: The team shipped it Tuesday.

notes: Style check, not hard ban: 'was killed' is flagged as possibly passive; rewrite active and direct.

title: Weasel words and hedge qualifiers
summary: 'Helps ensure', 'may be able to', 'can potentially' and weak quantifiers ('remarkably', 'few') either commit or cut; write-good flags them as weasel words.

source.rule: message="'{}' is hedging." items=("I would argue that", ", so to speak", "to a certain degree")
message: "Consider removing '%s'" tokens: appear to be / arguably / as far as I know / hopefully / in my opinion / more or less / presumably / probably / somewhat

tests.label: weasel qualifier fails
tests.input: The tool helps ensure uptime.

tests.label: committed claim passes
tests.input: The tool keeps the service up.

title: Weakening adverbs
summary: 'Very', 'really', 'extremely', 'simply', 'only' weaken the words they modify; write-good's adverb check flags them as 'can weaken meaning'.

source.rule: message=("Substitute 'damn' every time you're inclined to write 'very'; your editor will delete it and the writing will be just as it should be.") pattern=Padding.WORDS_IN_TEXT.format(r"very(?! well)")
message: "Consider removing '%s'" tokens: actually / basically / clearly / extremely / obviously / quite / remarkably / significantly / surprisingly / totally / very

tests.label: weakening adverb fails
tests.input: This sentence is simply terrible.

tests.label: strong word passes
tests.input: This sentence is broken.

notes: 'Only' and 'just' are purpose-gated: keep when they carry genuine contrast or limitation (e.g. 'read-only').

title: Wordy phrases
summary: 'As a matter of fact', 'in order to', 'due to the fact that' are wordy or unneeded; write-good's too-wordy check flags them.

source.rule: in order to=to / due to the fact that=due to|since / at this point in time=now / a number of=several|some / in the event that=if / with regard to=about / as a matter of fact=in fact|[OMIT]

CHECK_PATH = "misc.composition" "Omit needless words" items={"the question as to whether": "whether", "there is no doubt but that": "no doubt", "owing to the fact that": "because / since", "in spite of the fact that": "although / though", "he is a man who": "he", "in a hasty manner": "hastily", "the reason why is that": "because"}

tests.label: wordy phrase fails
tests.input: As a matter of fact, this could be simpler.

tests.label: concise phrasing passes
tests.input: This could be simpler.

title: Cliches
summary: Tired idioms ('at loose ends', 'avoid like the plague') are flagged as cliches by write-good; prefer plain wording.

source.rule: message: "'%s' is a cliché" tokens: - a chip off the old block / - a clean slate / - a far cry / - acid test / - against all odds

Idiom autopilot: double-edged sword, tip of the iceberg, elephant in the room, perfect storm, game changer, best of both worlds, win-win, paves the way, bridge the gap, at the forefront, uncharted territory, new normal, full circle, wild west | Pre-assembled phrase → disassemble

tests.label: cliche fails
tests.input: Writing specs puts me at loose ends.

tests.label: plain wording passes
tests.input: Writing specs is tedious.

title: Lexical illusions (repeated words)
summary: An immediately repeated word ('the the') is a typo-level defect write-good flags as 'is repeated'.

source.rule: pattern=Padding.STRICT_WORDS_IN_TEXT.format(r"(\w+(?:\s+\w+){0,3})(\s+\1)+") message="There's a lexical illusion in '{}' - a phrase is repeated."
extends: repetition message: "'%s' is repeated!" tokens: - '[\w]+'

tests.label: repeated word fails
tests.input: The the build failed.

tests.label: single occurrence passes
tests.input: The build failed.

title: 'So' sentence openers
summary: Starting a sentence with 'So' adds no meaning; write-good's so-check flags it except for 'So?' and mid-sentence uses.

source.rule: message: "Don't start a sentence with '%s'" raw: - '(?:[;-]\s)so[\s,]|So[\s,]'

tests.label: so opener fails
tests.input: So the best thing to do is wait.

tests.label: so? passes
tests.input: So?

tests.label: mid-sentence so passes
tests.input: This changes the code so that it works.

title: 'There is' / 'There are' openers
summary: Starting sentences with 'There is/are' is unnecessary verbiage; write-good flags it as 'unnecessary verbiage'.

source.rule: message: "Don't start a sentence with '%s'" raw: - '(?:^[^\w]*|[;-]\s)There\b\s(is|are)\b'

tests.label: there-is opener fails
tests.input: There is a use for this construction.

tests.label: direct subject passes
tests.input: This construction has a use.

title: No three consecutive same-length sentences
summary: Uniform sentence length is the single most measurable AI detection signal; three consecutive sentences of the same length are forbidden.

source.rule: No uniform sentence length (no three consecutive same-length sentences)
No uniform sentence length. No three consecutive sentences of the same length. Ever. Mix 4-word sentences with 30-word ones. This is the single most measurable AI detection signal.

tests.label: three same-length fails
tests.input: The gate opened. The gate closed. The gate jammed.

tests.label: mixed lengths pass
tests.input: The gate opened. It jammed again at noon, after the latch bent in the heat.

title: Burstiness: require short and long sentences
summary: Human writing alternates short punchy and long clause-heavy sentences; a 500-word block with no sentence under 8 or over 30 words lacks human burstiness.

source.rule: Sentence Length Uniformity (Burstiness) — Threshold: If a 500-word block contains no sentences under 8 words or over 30 words, it lacks human burstiness.

tests.label: mid-range cluster fails
tests.input: The service handles about fifteen thousand requests every hour. Each request passes through four separate internal queues. The slowest queue occasionally waits over two full seconds. Operators see a clean dashboard with every metric visible.

tests.label: short and long mix passes
tests.input: The service handles about fifteen thousand requests every hour, each passing through four internal queues before the slowest occasionally waits over two seconds. It works.

notes: Human baseline: 3+ distinct syntactic patterns per 100 words; AI text shows 1.5 or fewer.

title: Paragraph length uniformity
summary: AI aims for visual symmetry with paragraphs of nearly identical length; if all paragraphs in a section are within 15% of each other in word count, the section is likely AI-generated.

source.rule: Paragraph Length Uniformity — Threshold: If all paragraphs in a section are within 15% of each other in word count, the section is likely AI-generated.

tests.label: uniform paragraphs fail
tests.input: The queue drains at a steady two thousand messages per second once warm. Retries are handled by a separate worker that backs off on failure. Metrics are logged to the same store as the main pipeline. Alerts fire only when the lag exceeds ten seconds.

tests.label: varied paragraphs pass
tests.input: The queue drains at a steady two thousand messages per second once warm. Retries back off on failure. The alert only fires when lag exceeds ten seconds.

notes: Exception: bulleted lists, tables, and template fields are structurally uniform by design.

title: Transition density
summary: AI over-relies on transition words to maintain flow; if more than 30% of paragraphs begin with a transition word or adverbial clause, the text is structurally artificial.

source.rule: Transition Density — Threshold: If more than 30% of paragraphs in an article begin with a transition word or adverbial clause, the text is structurally artificial.

tests.label: transition-heavy fails
tests.input: However, the build is slow. Moreover, tests are flaky. Additionally, deploys stall. Thus the team avoids releases.

tests.label: few transitions pass
tests.input: The build is slow, and tests are flaky. The team avoids releases until both improve.

title: Opening-word repetition across paragraphs
summary: Three or more consecutive paragraphs starting with the same word or phrase pattern indicates mechanical generation; vary opening words.

source.rule: Several sentences in a row start with the same subject, often *she* or *he*, because repetition is handled by rule instead of by ear.
Opening-Word Repetition — Three or more consecutive paragraphs starting with the same word or phrase pattern indicates mechanical generation. Vary opening words.

tests.label: same opener three times fails
tests.input: The gate opens at nine. The gate closes at five. The gate alarms when forced.

tests.label: varied openers pass
tests.input: The gate opens at nine. By five it closes for the night. An alarm trips when forced.

title: Segmental entropy (flat pacing across sections)
summary: AI keeps flat stylistic consistency from introduction through conclusion; if sentence-length variance differs by less than 10% across intro, body, and conclusion, the text was likely generated in a single pass.

source.rule: Segmental Entropy — Threshold: Calculate sentence length variance separately for the introduction, body, and conclusion. If variance differs by less than 10% across all three segments, the text was likely generated as a single pass by AI.

tests.label: monotone sections fail
tests.input: The gate opens at nine and closes at five. It uses a latch that trips an alarm. The latch is replaced each spring. The alarm reports to a central panel.

tests.label: register shift passes
tests.input: The gate opens at nine and closes at five. It uses a latch that trips an alarm, and the latch is replaced each spring so the alarm keeps reporting to the central panel. The gate works.

notes: Human introductions are tighter and more declarative; body sections are denser; conclusions shift register.

title: Hedging density
summary: AI models hedge 4-7x more than human writers (ACL 2024, 12,000 documents); more than 3 hedging markers per paragraph or 8 per 1,000 words in declarative sections indicates generation.

source.rule: Hedging and epistemic modality overload (thresholds: 3/paragraph, 8 per 1,000 words)

Hedging Thresholds — Per-paragraph: More than 3 hedging instances in a single paragraph warrants scrutiny. Per-1000-words: More than 8 hedging markers per 1,000 words in declarative sections (Background, History, Timeline) indicates AI generation.

tests.label: hedge stack fails
tests.input: The fix may work, but it might introduce issues that could affect other systems, and it seems likely the tradeoffs are probably acceptable.

tests.label: grounded hedge passes
tests.input: The FTC's 2024 enforcement data suggests a 12% increase.

notes: Do not flag hedging in sections discussing pending legislation, ongoing litigation, or genuinely disputed facts. Markers: may, might, could, potentially, probably, generally, usually, arguably, likely, it seems, it appears, unclear, remains to be seen.

title: Hallucinated markup artifacts
summary: oaicite, contentReference, grok_card, attributableIndex, and turn0search0 are AI citation placeholders leaked from training data; any occurrence means unedited AI output. Zero tolerance.

tests.label: leaked placeholder fails
tests.input: The bill passed [oaicite:1] with broad support.

tests.label: clean citation passes
tests.input: The bill passed in July with broad support.

title: Excessive bold / mid-sentence emphasis
summary: Bold sprinkled mid-sentence or repeatedly is formatting slop; bold a term once at most when introducing it and let the words do the work.

source.rule: Formatting restraint: do not bold excessively
Words are bolded without a reason, and vertical lists give every item a bold label and a colon.

tests.label: repeated bold fails
tests.input: The **gate** is **broken** and **jammed**.

tests.label: no bold passes
tests.input: The gate is broken and jammed.

title: Emoji bullets, headings, and stacks
summary: Every line starting with an emoji, emoji in headings, and emoji used as bullet points is slop; one or two emoji per post is the ceiling.

source.rule: Formatting restraint: do not use emoji unless asked

tests.label: emoji bullet stack fails
tests.input: ✅ Fast ✅ Reliable ✅ Cheap

tests.label: plain list passes
tests.input: Fast, reliable, and cheap.

title: Bullet list overuse
summary: Excessive bullet points are an AI formatting default; never more than 5-7 in a row, and if it fits in a sentence, use a sentence.

source.rule: No excessive bullet points (never more than 5-7 in a row)
Formatting slop: bullet lists where two sentences of prose would read better

tests.label: ten bullets fail
tests.input:
- one
- two
- three
- four
- five
- six
- seven
- eight
- nine
- ten

tests.label: three bullets pass
tests.input:
- one
- two
- three

title: Markdown in plain-text contexts
summary: Asterisks and headers rendering as symbols in emails, DMs, and SMS is an instant AI tell; no markdown in plain-text contexts.

source.rule: No markdown in plain text contexts (emails, DMs, SMS)

tests.label: markdown in DM fails
tests.input: Great work *so far*!

tests.label: plain text passes
tests.input: Great work so far.

notes: Also: no markdown headers in social media, emails, or casual writing — an instant AI flag.

title: 'Thread:' and '🧵' openers
summary: Opening a post with 'Thread:' or the thread emoji is a social-media AI tell; content should make people keep reading on its own.

tests.label: thread opener fails
tests.input: Thread: what I learned shipping v2

tests.label: substance opener passes
tests.input: What I learned shipping v2

title: Hashtag stacks
summary: A stack of hashtags is a social-media AI tell; zero to two, integrated naturally.

source.rule: No hashtag stacks (zero to two, integrated naturally)

tests.label: hashtag stack fails
tests.input: Shipping the dashboard today #build #dev #startup #ai #growth

tests.label: no hashtags passes
tests.input: Shipping the dashboard today.

title: Heading anti-patterns
summary: Narrative, dramatic, or clickbait headings ('The [Concept] Trap', 'The Hidden Danger', 'Why X Destroys Y', vague analytical labels) read like thriller titles; headings must describe the section content.

source.rule: Rule 16: No narrative, dramatic, or AI-generic headings

Banned Heading Structures — "The [Concept] Trap" | "The [Adjective] [Noun]" drama | "The [Noun] [Dramatic Noun]" | "Why [Action] [Dramatic Verb] [Object]" | "[Noun]: The [Adjective] [Noun]" | "The [Noun] You [Emotion Verb]"

tests.label: dramatic heading fails
tests.input: ## The Hidden Danger

tests.label: descriptive heading passes
tests.input: ## Firmware Corruption After Sudden Power Loss

notes: A good heading reads like a technical manual index entry: specific, descriptive, and boring to non-specialists. Includes parenthetical-clarification ban (see ZS-PROSE-068).

title: Sentence case in headings
summary: Title case in headings beyond the first word and proper nouns is formatting slop; use sentence case.

source.rule: Formatting restraint: no title case in headings beyond the first word and proper nouns
Headings capitalize every main word ... Use sentence case, remove the decoration and the rules, and let the title stand once.

tests.label: title case fails
tests.input: ## This Is Title Case

tests.label: sentence case passes
tests.input: ## This is sentence case

notes: Proper nouns are exempt; triage should not flag '## Apple Vision Pro'.

title: 'Key takeaways' sections
summary: 'Key takeaways' and 'TL;DR' recap sections are banned structural formulas; end on the last concrete point instead.

source.rule: Formatting restraint: do not create 'key takeaways' sections

tests.label: takeaways section fails
tests.input:
## Key Takeaways
The gate opens at nine.

tests.label: concrete section passes
tests.input:
## Hours
The gate opens at nine.

title: Exclusion zones for lexical scans
summary: Lexical scans must not flag text inside direct quotes from cited sources, titles, names, verbatim values, or code/markup shown as examples; severity drops when a banned word sits next to named entities.

source.rule: False positive prevention (exclusion zones, context-aware severity, metaphorical vs. literal)

tests.label: quoted source excluded
tests.input: She said, "let's delve into it" in the meeting.

tests.label: banned word outside quotes fails
tests.input: Let's delve into the archive.

notes: Higher severity: 'a comprehensive examination of the issues' (abstract, no specifics). Lower severity: 'comprehensive audit by the FTC in 2024' (specific entity and date). Metaphorical-vs-literal bigram checks apply to ecosystem, landscape, navigate, tapestry, symphony, beacon, testament.

title: Parenthetical clarifications in headings
summary: Headings with parenthetical suffixes (counts, labels, dates) read as meta-commentary instead of naming the section subject.

source.rule: Rule 3: No parenthetical clarifications in headings

tests.label: parenthetical heading fails
tests.input: ## Migration (IMPORTANT)

tests.label: plain heading passes
tests.input: ## Migration

notes: Multiline + no-cross-line heading text: pattern must not swallow prose up to the first parenthesis.

title: Repeated talking points
summary: Saying the same point twice is padding; duplicates are filler.

tests.label: restated point fails
tests.input: The gate is slow. Again, the gate is slow.

tests.label: single statement passes
tests.input: The gate is slow.

title: Identical paragraph layout runs
summary: Three consecutive sections or paragraphs with identical layout (topic sentence, explanation, example, transition) is a pattern; break it.

source.rule: Rule 7: Vary structure (three consecutive identical layouts is a pattern)
No identical paragraph structure / no parallel structure across sections
Symmetric scaffolding. Every paragraph the same length, every section a header plus three bullets, every list item the same grammatical shape. Fix: break the grid where the content doesn't need it.

tests.label: identical layouts fail
tests.input: The queue drains fast. It uses four workers. For example, the log shows 2k/s. The queue drains fast. It uses four workers. For example, the log shows 2k/s. The queue drains fast. It uses four workers. For example, the log shows 2k/s.

tests.label: varied layouts pass
tests.input: The queue drains fast. Four workers drain it at 2k/s. The log proves it.

title: 'Challenges and future prospects' endings
summary: Ending a piece with a section about challenges faced and future outlook is a structural AI formula; weave challenges into the body instead.

tests.label: outlook section fails
tests.input:
## Challenges and Future Prospects
We face flaky tests.

tests.label: body-integrated passes
tests.input:
## Failures We Fixed
Flaky tests now retry twice.

title: Generic filler (portability test)
summary: A sentence that could move unchanged to another person, company, country, or product is filler; every claim must end with a concrete, verifiable detail or be deleted.

source.rule: Use the portability test; be concrete and specific
Rule 5: No hollow statements; Rule 13: Write like a researcher, not a copywriter

tests.label: portable filler fails
tests.input: In today's competitive market, companies must innovate to stay ahead.

tests.label: grounded claim passes
tests.input: Our queue depth hit 40,000 last Tuesday, so we added two workers.

title: False agency: inanimate subject with human verb
summary: Unslop and stop-slop flag handing rhetorical agency to inanimate things so the writer can assert significance without claiming it: 'the data tells a story', 'the market believes'. The data does not narrate; state the finding and the actor.

tests.label: data tells a story fails
tests.input: The data tells a clear story of decline.

tests.label: literal figure passes
tests.input: Revenue fell 12% in Q3.

notes: Covers cognitive verbs (decides, believes, argues, hopes, warns...). Weaker verbs like 'shows/suggests/indicates' are left to ZS-PROSE-012 and legit usage ('the chart shows...').

title: Tool/system anthropomorphism
summary: Unslop's tool-anthropomorphism tell: marketing hands an inanimate tool volitional agency — 'the bench decides', 'the scanner wants'. A tool does not decide, hunt, want, know, or judge; name the mechanism instead.

tests.label: scanner decides fails
tests.input: The scanner decides which files to flag.

tests.label: mechanical verb passes
tests.input: The linter checks every file for style errors.

notes: Ordinary technical register is spared: 'the parser reads the file', 'the gate fails the build'. Volitional verbs (decides, wants, knows, believes, judges) are the tell.

title: '<abstract noun> is real' closers
summary: Unslop's emphasis crutch: 'The struggle is real', 'The stakes are real' asserts stakes instead of naming the concrete consequence. The '<abstract noun> is/are real' frame inflates significance without evidence.

source.rule: Emphasis Crutches / The X is real

tests.label: struggle is real fails
tests.input: The struggle is real.

tests.label: specific claim passes
tests.input: Three prototypes failed before the design held.

notes: Spares the literal 'is it genuine?' sense; the rule is about the rhetorical closer, not factual claims about reality.

title: Colon reveals ('The answer is:')
summary: Unslop's colon-overuse pattern: 'The answer is: [reveal]', 'The key takeaway: [point]' — the setup-then-reveal colon performs drama instead of stating the point directly. Regex subset of the dramatic-colon tell.

tests.label: answer-is-colon fails
tests.input: The answer is: ship faster.

tests.label: no colon passes
tests.input: The answer is that speed matters less than trust.

notes: Complement to ZS-PROSE-022 (dramatic colon in general); this rule covers the specific 'The X is:' family that has a machine-checkable shape.

title: Escape-hatch family ('less about X than Y', 'the real X is')
summary: Deslopify's negative-parallelism regexes: 'less about X than Y', 'the question isn't whether...', and unslop's throat-clearer 'The real [X] is' all frame a point by rejecting a foil, implying prior deception without evidence.

matcher.pattern: \b(?:less about [^.!?;]{2,60} than (?:about )?|the (?:question|point|issue|problem|goal) is(n'?t| not) (?:whether|about|just|if)|the real (?:challenge|problem|issue|question|goal|story|test|battle|winner|enemy) is)\b

tests.label: less about fails
tests.input: This is less about speed than about trust.

tests.label: real X is fails
tests.input: The real problem is the onboarding flow.

tests.label: direct claim passes
tests.input: Onboarding takes two weeks, which blocks new users.

notes: Distinct from ZS-PROSE-024 (period-separated 'The question is X. The question is Y') — this covers the comma/than-forms and the 'real X' opener.

title: Copula-avoidance cluster (constitutes/functions/operates/acts as)
summary: Unslop's copula avoidance: AI substitutes fancier verbs for 'is/are' — 'constitutes a', 'functions as', 'operates as'. Extends the fake-strong copula family (ZS-PROSE-031) with the nominalizing variants.

tests.label: cluster fails
tests.input: The tool constitutes a complete solution. It functions as a dashboard and operates as a gateway.

tests.label: plain copula passes
tests.input: The tool is a complete solution with a dashboard and a gateway.

notes: 'serves as' / 'stands as' already banned by ZS-PROSE-031; this rule adds the remaining members of unslop's copula table. Warning tier: a single use in formal prose is normal.

title: Future-narrative closers ('may become the most important story')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's future-narrative pattern: vague future significance with no falsifiable claim — 'may become one of the most important narratives', 'one of the most important stories of the coming decade'.

tests.label: modal become narrative fails
tests.input: This may become one of the most important narratives of the next decade.

tests.label: concrete outcome passes
tests.input: The feature shipped this week and early metrics look good.

title: Hedge-stacked predictions ('could potentially', 'may eventually')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's hedge-stack: stacking a modal with a hedge adverb — 'could potentially create', 'may eventually unlock'. Either word alone is fine; the stack is the tell.

tests.label: could potentially fails
tests.input: The policy could potentially create new opportunities.

tests.label: may eventually fails
tests.input: It may eventually unlock value.

tests.label: single hedge passes
tests.input: The policy could create new opportunities, or it may not.

notes: The negative lookahead spares plain negation ('could not possibly') and ordinary question inversion. Extends ZS-PROSE-043's single-term bans with the stacked-modal shape.

title: Social endorsement closers ('worth your time', 'do yourself a favor')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's social-CTA closer and unslop's vague endorsements: 'worth your time', 'do yourself a favor and read this', 'thank me later' — a recommendation performed without a reason to click.

terms: do yourself a favor and read
do yourself a favour and read
you won't want to miss this
you will not want to miss this
do yourself a favor and watch
do yourself a favor and check out

tests.label: worth your time fails
tests.input: This one is worth your time: read the full report.

tests.label: specific reason passes
tests.input: The report explains why prices rose.

notes: Warning tier: fine when the recommendation carries a specific reason; the bare curatorial sign-off is the tell.

title: Infomercial hooks ('here's the kicker', 'the catch?')
summary: Deslop's 'Here's the Kicker' and deslopify's hook regexes: false-suspense transitions ('here's the kicker', 'here's the catch', 'the twist?') that promise a revelation for a point that needed no buildup.

terms: here is where it gets interesting

tests.label: kicker fails
tests.input: Here's the kicker: the free tier is gone.

tests.label: direct statement passes
tests.input: The free tier is gone.

notes: 'here's the thing' is already covered by ZS-PROSE-009; this rule covers the kicker/catch/twist family.

title: Vague declaratives ('the implications are significant')
summary: Stop-slop's vague declaratives: sentences that announce importance without naming the specific thing — 'The implications are significant', 'The stakes are high', 'The consequences are real'.

tests.label: implications significant fails
tests.input: The implications are significant.

tests.label: specific outcome passes
tests.input: The change cut deployment time by 40%.

title: Lazy extremes (everyone/nobody knows, always/never works)
summary: Stop-slop's lazy extremes and unslop's absolute words: sweeping claims — 'everyone knows', 'nobody believes', 'this never works' — assert false authority where specifics would do.

tests.label: everyone knows fails
tests.input: Everyone knows that shortcuts fail.

tests.label: never works fails
tests.input: That never works in production.

tests.label: scoped claim passes
tests.input: Our team never ships on Fridays.

notes: Warning tier: purpose-gate — 'never'/'always' are legitimate in safety, security, legal, and technical rules (per unslop's core contract).

title: Meta-joiners ('in this section, we'll')
summary: Stop-slop's meta-commentary: announcing structure instead of delivering it — 'In this section, we'll...', 'Let me walk you through...'. Extends ZS-PROSE-015's collaborative narrator list with the section/chapter forms.

terms: let us take a look at

tests.label: section joiner fails
tests.input: In this section, we'll cover the basics.

tests.label: direct content passes
tests.input: The basics come first.

title: Negative countdown ('Not X. Not Y. Just Z.')
summary: Deslop's countdown and stop-slop's negative listing: 'Not ten. Not fifty. Just five hundred and twenty-three' builds false tension by negating before revealing. State the point directly.

source.rule: Not X. Not Y. Just Z.
Negative Parallelisms / No X, no Y, just Z

tests.label: countdown fails
tests.input: Not ten. Not fifty. Just five hundred and twenty-three.

tests.label: lowercase countdown fails
tests.input: No fast fixes, no magic pills, just steady work.

tests.label: plain statement passes
tests.input: Ten failed, then fifty, then five hundred and twenty-three passed.

notes: Extends ZS-PROSE-025 (article forms 'Not a X. Not a Y.') to article-free countdowns and the 'no X, no Y, just Z' payoff.

title: Self-posed rhetorical reveal ('The result? Devastating.')
summary: Deslop's 'The X? A Y.' pattern: the model asks a question nobody asked, then answers it for dramatic effect — 'The result? Devastating.', 'The worst part? Nobody saw it coming.'

tests.label: result question fails
tests.input: The result? Devastating.

tests.label: plain statement passes
tests.input: The result of the test surprised everyone.

title: Tricolon pattern-stacking (2+ triads per 150 words)
summary: Deslopify's rule-of-three regex and deslop's tricolon abuse: LLMs default to 'X, Y, and Z' triplets to make thin analysis look thorough. One triad is voice; stacked triads are a pattern-recognition failure.

tests.label: stacked triads fail
tests.input: The tool is fast, reliable, and affordable. It stays simple, clean, and efficient.

tests.label: single triad passes
tests.input: We offer fast, reliable, and affordable hosting.

notes: Machine-checkable complement to ZS-PROSE-026 (rule-of-three overuse, semantic). Cap: at most one 'X, Y, and Z' triad per 150 words.

title: Tier-1A AI frequency markers
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's Tier 1A vocabulary: words that appear far more often in AI text ('embark', 'deep dive', 'unpack', 'holistic', 'impactful', 'meticulous', 'ever-evolving'). Always flag; replace on sight.

tests.label: 1A stack fails
tests.input: We embark on a deep dive into the complexities of this market.

tests.label: plain language passes
tests.input: We looked at the problem for a week before shipping.

notes: The tier's own caveat (from the source): the 5-20x ratio is inherited from brandonwise/humanizer and unverified here. Delve-class words already banned by ZS-PROSE-001/002/003; 'absolutely' by ZS-PROSE-004.

title: Tier-1B clarity edits (commence, ascertain, wordy phrases)
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's Tier 1B: wordiness and inflated formality — 'commence', 'ascertain', 'is able to', 'a large number of'. A 1B hit is a clarity edit, not evidence of machine authorship.

source.rule: Filler Adverbs & Phrases (is able to, a large number of)

tests.label: wordy verbs fail
tests.input: We will commence the audit to ascertain compliance.

tests.label: plain verbs pass
tests.input: We will start the audit to check compliance.

notes: 'utilize', 'in order to', 'due to the fact that' already banned by ZS-PROSE-001/045.

title: Tier-2 vocabulary cluster (2+ per paragraph)
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's Tier 2: individually fine words ('harness', 'navigate', 'foster', 'empower') that signal AI when two or more appear in the same paragraph.

source.rule: Tier 2 - flag when 2+ appear in the same paragraph

tests.label: cluster fails
tests.input: We harness data to navigate complexity and empower every team.

tests.label: sparse usage passes
tests.input: The build pipeline runs every commit through the test suite. Failures block the merge and the team fixes them within the hour. Release notes come from commit messages and the changelog stays current. Nobody owns the docs, so they drift.

notes: Density cap approximates the source's '2+ per paragraph': at most one Tier-2 word per 40 words. Streamline/facilitate/bolster/foster etc. already banned outright by ZS-PROSE-001.

title: Tier-3 vocabulary density (>=3% of words)
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's Tier 3: normal words ('significant', 'innovative', 'effective', 'compelling') that AI overuses; flag only at high density (~3% of words) — vague praise instead of specifics.

tests.label: dense praise fails
tests.input: The update is a significant change with an innovative approach to caching. The team calls it a compelling story: the system is more scalable and effective under load. Exceptional results follow and the improvement is remarkable. We measured throughput directly.

tests.label: scattered usage passes
tests.input: The update changes how the cache stores hot keys. Throughput rose 34% under the load test, and the team kept the change behind a feature flag for a week. The changelog lists three fixes and one new endpoint. We measured the improvement with a benchmark run on the staging cluster before rolling it out to production. The cache stores hot keys in memory and evicts cold entries to disk.

notes: Density cap: at most 3 Tier-3 words per 100 words (~3%). 'Significantly' and 'remarkably' already banned outright by ZS-PROSE-004/043.

title: Unfilled placeholder slots ('[Your Name]', '[INSERT X]')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's AI-placeholder fingerprint: unfilled directive stubs — '[Your Name]', '[Insert source URL]', '[DESCRIBE...]' — left in published text; a near-definitive AI-tool signature.

tests.label: your-name stub fails
tests.input: [Insert your company name here] delivers results.

tests.label: no stub passes
tests.input: The company delivers results.

notes: Integrity-adjacent (unpublished template), but kept in prose because the trigger is a plain-text pattern. Bracketed code identifiers and citation refs are excluded by the verb-led capture.

title: False concession structures ('While X is impressive, Y remains a challenge')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's and unslop's false concession: simulated balance — 'While X is impressive, Y remains a challenge', 'it is not without its challenges' — that never names the actual tradeoff.

tests.label: while-remains fails
tests.input: While the framework is impressive, adoption remains a challenge.

tests.label: specific tradeoff passes
tests.input: Adoption lags because the framework lacks examples.

title: Rhetorical question openers ('So why should you care?', 'What's next?')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's and unslop's rhetorical-question openers: 'So why should you care?', 'But what does this mean for...', 'What's next?' — engagement bait that stalls instead of making the point.

tests.label: why should you care fails
tests.input: So why should you care? Because the numbers matter.

tests.label: direct reason passes
tests.input: The numbers matter because they change the budget.

title: Speculative scenario openers ('Imagine a world where')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's and deslop's speculative openers: 'Imagine a world where...', 'Picture a future in which...' — an argument opened with a hypothetical list of desirable outcomes instead of a claim.

tests.label: imagine a world fails
tests.input: Imagine a world where every tool has a quiet intelligence behind it.

tests.label: teaching example passes
tests.input: Imagine you have an array of ten items.

notes: The source explicitly spares instructional 'imagine you have X' examples; the tell is the world/future/reality + where/whereby framing.

title: Formulaic emergence claims ('has emerged as a key...', 'has become increasingly...')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's formulaic openers: 'has emerged as a leading/ key/ major...', 'has become increasingly important' — pseudo-significance that states nothing specific about the subject.

source.rule: Formulaic openers (has emerged as a leading...)

tests.label: emerged as key fails
tests.input: Rust has emerged as a key player in systems programming.

tests.label: specific fact passes
tests.input: Rust is now used in the Linux kernel.

notes: Gated to the inflated nouns (leading, key, major...) so bare 'has emerged as a' (ordinary English) stays clean, per the source's own gating.

title: Confidence-calibration stacking (3+ per piece)
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's confidence-calibration pattern: 'interestingly', 'surprisingly', 'importantly', 'undoubtedly' — sentence-level meta-commentary that performs thoughtfulness; only flagged when it stacks (3+ per piece).

tests.label: stack of three fails
tests.input: Interestingly, the data holds. Importantly, the pattern repeats. Notably, it does so everywhere.

tests.label: no commentary passes
tests.input: The data holds, and the pattern repeats everywhere.

title: Parenthetical hedging asides ('(and increasingly, X)', '(though to be fair, Y)')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's and unslop's parenthetical hedging: pseudo-asides that add no information but perform thoughtfulness — '(and increasingly, cheaper)', '(or more precisely, Y)', '(though to be fair, Z)'.

tests.label: parenthetical hedge fails
tests.input: The design is simpler (and increasingly, cheaper) to run.

tests.label: plain clause passes
tests.input: The design is simpler and cheaper to run.

title: Slot-fill template phrases ('a [adjective] step forward for...')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's template phrases: slot-fill constructions where a blank could go and still sound the same — 'a significant step forward for', 'I recently had the pleasure of'. The 'Whether you're X or Y' member is already covered by ZS-PROSE-016.

tests.label: step forward fails
tests.input: The release is a significant step forward for the platform.

tests.label: specifics pass
tests.input: The release adds batch processing and keyboard shortcuts.

title: Generic positive conclusions ('The future looks bright')
summary: Unslop's, avoid-ai-writing's, and human-writing's generic conclusions: 'The future looks bright', 'Exciting times lie ahead', 'Only time will tell' — content-free optimism that ends the piece on a shrug.

terms: a step in the right direction

source.rule: Generic Positive Conclusion — "The future looks bright", "Exciting times lie ahead", "This is a major step in the right direction". Rule: R-36
Hedged non-endings. "Despite these challenges, the future looks bright"; conclusions that restate the piece; both-sidesing that refuses to land on a position.

tests.label: future looks bright fails
tests.input: The future looks bright for the company.

tests.label: concrete plan passes
tests.input: The company plans two more locations next year.

title: False ranges ('from X to Y, from A to B')
summary: Deslop's, unslop's, and human-writing's false ranges: 'from X to Y, from A to B' and 'spanning everything from...' where the endpoints aren't on a meaningful scale — a fancy way to list two loosely related things.

tests.input: The book covers the Big Bang and star formation.

title: Numbered list inflation ('Here are 7 reasons...')
summary: Unslop's numbered-list inflation: 'Three key takeaways', 'Here are 7 reasons...', 'Top seven' — the number is chosen for format, not meaning; AI overuses counted lists because they're structurally safe.

tests.label: seven reasons fails
tests.input: Here are 7 reasons why this matters.

tests.label: word count passes
tests.input: There are two main reasons for the change.

title: Emotional flatline ('What struck me was...', 'the most interesting part')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's emotional-flatline patterns: 'What surprised me most', 'What struck me was', 'the most interesting part/thing' — performative reactions that substitute for a specific observation.

tests.label: struck me fails

tests.label: plain fact passes

title: Lingering-attention claims ('the line I keep coming back to')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's lingering-attention patterns: 'the line I keep coming back to', 'I can't stop thinking about' — share-post openers that claim duration of attention instead of saying anything about the thing.

tests.label: keep coming back fails

tests.label: specific content passes
tests.input: Her keynote covered three case studies.

title: Novelty inflation ('coined the phrase', 'a problem nobody talks about')
summary: Avoid-ai-writing's and unslop's novelty inflation: 'introduced a term', 'coined the phrase', 'a problem nobody talks about' — framing routine ideas as secret discoveries. 'What nobody tells you' already covered by ZS-PROSE-010.

terms: a problem no one talks about

tests.label: coined phrase fails

tests.label: plain attribution passes

title: CJK binary-contrast shell (不是A而是B / 不在于A而在于B)
summary: De-ai-writing's 二分对照壳: the lecture-style correction frame '不是A而是B' / '不在于A而在于B' / '并非A而是B' that presents a reframe as a surprise reveal. Default to clearing; state the positive claim directly.

tests.label: not-but shell fails

title: CJK signpost words (路标词)
summary: De-ai-writing's 路标词: '更关键', '换句话说', '事实上', '值得注意', '与此同时', '不可否认', '毋庸置疑' — textbook connectors that announce structure instead of delivering content; max 2 total per piece per the source.
